title: Kabir close
hookLine: a weaver who argued with priests and pirs and loved the Lord more than both

cards: What do you call a man who tells a learned Brahmin to his face that birth makes no one higher, and then calls himself the Lord's dog? Fierce? Humble?

Kabir's hymns won't let you pick one. He was a weaver of Benares who argued with the pandit on one side and the qazi on the other, and loved the Lord more than either argument. Today the threads lie side by side.

teach.h: A WEAVER, AND THE WORLD AS CLOTH.
teach.b: First, the weaver. Kabir worked the loom, a julaha, and he pictured the body and the whole world as cloth, warp and weft, with the Lord as the weaver.
When his mother wept that he sang instead of weaving, his answer was that the one Lord is the giver, for him and for the children too. Second, the arguments.

teach.h: TO THE BRAHMIN AND THE QAZI.
teach.b: To the Brahmin he says, in paraphrase: you are a Brahmin and I'm a weaver of Kashi; try to understand my wisdom. To the qazi he asks which book it is he's explaining.
And he asked the man proud of high birth why he hadn't come into the world by some other road. Yet he told both not to call the scriptures false. False, he said, is the one who doesn't reflect.
The argument was never with the books. It was with pride wearing the books like a robe. Third, the love underneath.
When he described himself, it wasn't as a champion.

teach.h: WORST OF ALL, THE LORD'S DOG.
teach.b: He was the worst of all, and everyone else was good. He was the Lord's dog, led on a chain. An elephant, in his hymn, bowed instead of charging.
He spoke of dying to the ego while alive, went to Maghar because the place doesn't save you, and sang at home, to Loi.
Lay those threads together and a pattern shows: his fierceness and his humility are the same cloth.

He could be blunt with the powerful because he expected nothing from them, and humble before everyone else because he expected everything from the Lord. The Gurus kept his hymns in the Granth, and Sikhs sing them still.

how: Kabir's hymns and saloks are part of the Guru Granth Sahib, sung in kirtan and read in gurdwaras alongside the Gurus' own words, and Sikhs honor him as a bhagat whose devotion the Gurus recognized.

o: a court poet who sang the praises of the kings of Benares
a Brahmin scholar who taught the old scriptures in Kashi
the weaver of Benares, blunt with pride, humble before the Lord

games.q: the Kabir days — tap the pairs.
p: asked which book he was explaining
the one he spoke to at home

s: Kabir told the Brahmin and the qazi their scriptures were false
he said not to call them false; false is the one who doesn't reflect.
Kabir called himself the Lord's dog, led on a chain
his humility sits in the same cloth as his fierceness.
Kabir's hymns are kept in the Guru Granth Sahib
the Gurus kept them, and Sikhs sing them still.

games.q: you've spent these days with Kabir: blunt with the proud, low before everyone else. how do the two fit?
o: they don't; he had two moods.
one cloth: he expected nothing from the powerful and everything from the Lord.
he was humble only in private.
games.why: his fierceness and his humility are the same cloth: blunt with pride because he needed nothing from it, humble because he looked to the Lord for everything.

practice: Picture your day as cloth on a loom: the long threads already set, work, meals, errands, the people you'll pass.

Choose one cross-thread to pull through, one kind act tucked into something you were doing anyway, like holding a door, asking a real question or clearing someone else's cup, and see the moment it fits.
If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Kabir. The weaver of Benares who signs his saloks with his own name: blunt with pride, humble before people, devoted to the Lord.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the name that opens his saloks, like a signature.

carryVoice: Your line: weave it in. Fierce and humble, one cloth. Seven hundred sixty days, and counting.
